ParaBlock.RichText:
Imagine you work in a retail company’s IT team, and you want to stop suspicious login attempts before they cause harm. Machine learning can help you. You start by using training data—past examples of both safe and unsafe logins—to help a computer learn what to look for. This process is called supervised learning, where the system learns from labeled examples.
Behind the scenes, the computer uses algorithms, or step-by-step instructions, to find patterns in the login data. These patterns are stored in data sets and used to train a classification model—a tool that sorts new logins into categories like “safe” or “suspicious.” When something looks off, like a login at 3 a.m. from a new location, the model flags it as an anomaly, helping you catch potential threats early.

In today's data-driven world, security teams are faced with an overwhelming volume of security data. Machine learning is a powerful tool that can help them analyze this data and identify patterns that may indicate potential threats.

ParaBlock.RichText: Machine learning helps cybersecurity systems get smarter over time—spotting and responding to new threats quickly, often in real time. Here’s a simple breakdown of how machine learning models are trained to detect threats.

Tabs.Instructions: Click on each tab to learn more

Content.RichText: Gather a wide range of real-world digital activity and threat examples.
Clean up the data and organize it so the system can understand it.
Choose the most effective method for spotting threats or patterns.
Let the system analyze the data and learn what normal (and abnormal) behavior looks like.
Check how well the system’s predictions work in action.
Put the trained model to work in real cybersecurity environments.
Regularly update the model with new data, so it adapts to changing threats.

ParaBlock.RichText: Even if you’re not setting up or training cybersecurity systems yourself, it’s important to know how machine learning tools work. By understanding what goes into making these tools effective, you’ll be more aware of how cyber risks are managed behind the scenes, why security updates matter, and how you can support a safer, smarter workplace in your day-to-day role.

Even with the best training, there are always new risks. Anomaly detection lets machine learning tools spot activity that stands out from the usual pattern, helping catch things no one has seen before.
For example: If an employee downloads large amounts of data at midnight—something they’ve never done—this activity is flagged as an anomaly. These alerts help security teams quickly investigate and stop possible breaches, even if it’s a brand-new tactic that’s never been labeled before.
Anomaly detectors safeguard network traffic by identifying unusual patterns that could signal security threats. Learn more about their important role in cybersecurity.

Web.altText: Importance of anomaly detectors are early threat detection, proactive security, protecting private information, and safe operations.​ All text included in the image is Block 1. Spot problems early. Quickly find unusual activity, like strange logins or big file downloads, so issues can be caught before they turn into bigger problems. Block 2. Act fast on threats. Send alerts right away if something suspicious happens, so your IT team can respond and stop threats quickly.​ Block 3. Protect private information. Keep sensitive data, like employee or customer records, safe by catching risky behavior or break ins as soon as they happen.​ Block 4. Keep systems running safely. Watch for anything out of the ordinary on the network, helping to keep computers and services working the way they should.​

Item.ItemPara: Machine learning models use training data and algorithms to learn patterns in normal and suspicious behavior.

Once trained, these models use classification and anomaly detection to flag unusual activity that could signal a cybersecurity threat.
